title: The pedigree of the horses; Pandarus’ second boast
intro: Diomedes explains why Aeneas’ horses are worth capturing: they descend from the team Zeus gave Tros. The genealogical digression delays the duel, after which Pandarus repeats his mistake of announcing victory too soon.

notes.text: The infinitives continue Diomedes’ commands to Sthenelus: rush at Aeneas’ horses and drive them away. μεμνημένος is perfect middle/passive participle of μιμνήσκω, ‘remembering,’ with genitive ἵππων. ἐλάσαι is aorist infinitive of ἐλαύνω. μετά with accusative marks the destination among the Greeks; ἐϋκνήμιδας means ‘well-greaved.’

Τρωΐ is dative singular of Τρώς, the ancestral king Tros, not a plural ‘Trojans.’ δῶχ᾽ is elided δῶκε with aspiration before the following rough breathing: Zeus gave horses as compensation (ποινήν) for Ganymede. υἷος is genitive singular of υἱός, ‘son.’ The horses’ divine origin explains their extraordinary value.

The genitive γενεῆς marks stock or descent. The relative ἧς continues that pedigree, with horses understood as what Zeus gave. ἵππων is partitive with ἄριστοι. ἔασιν is epic third plural of εἰμί. ‘Under dawn and sun’ is expansive poetic language for the whole world, not a technical geographical boundary.

Anchises ‘stole’ a share of the bloodline by secretly breeding mares with Laomedon’s stallions. ὑποσχών is aorist participle of ὑπέχω, literally ‘putting under,’ not the promise verb ὑπισχνέομαι. θήλεας is feminine accusative plural, ‘female.’ γενέθλη, ‘offspring / stock,’ is a collective expression for the six foals born to him.

ἀτίταλλε is imperfect of ἀτιτάλλω, ‘rear, tend carefully,’ with φάτνη, ‘manger.’ μήστωρε is accusative dual of μήστωρ, ‘expert / master’; φόβοιο denotes flight or rout. The phrase praises the pair’s skill in battlefield movement. τούτω is accusative dual after λάβοιμεν, ‘if we captured these two.’

λάβοιμεν is first-plural second-aorist active optative of λαμβάνω. ἀροίμεθα is aorist middle optative of ἀείρω, ‘win for ourselves,’ the plural counterpart of ἄροιτο on page 5.1. κεν marks the prospective possibility: capturing the team would win noble renown. The horses are a source of κλέος as well as material wealth.

The pronouns distinguish the two conversations: Diomedes and Sthenelus were speaking while the Trojan pair drew near. τώ is nominative dual, but ἦλθον is plural; ἐλαύνοντε is dual again. Such shifts are normal epic usage. πρότερος makes Pandarus the first speaker, as he will also be first to cast.

καρτερόθυμος means ‘stout-hearted’; δαΐφρων, ‘warlike / skilled in war,’ is another vocative. δαμάσσατο is aorist middle of δαμάζω, ‘subdued.’ πειρήσομαι is future middle of πειράω, ‘try.’ τύχωμι is epic first-singular aorist subjunctive of τυγχάνω: ‘to see if I can hit,’ with αἴ κε.

ἀμπεπαλών is a reduplicated aorist participle of ἀναπάλλω, ‘brandish,’ with ἀμ- for ἀνα-. προΐει is imperfect of προΐημι, ‘cast.’ πταμένη is aorist middle participle of πέτομαι, agreeing with αἰχμή, ‘spear-point.’ πελάσθη is aorist passive of πελάζω, ‘came up against,’ with dative θώρηκι. The point reaches armour; the narrator does not say it pierces Diomedes’ body.

βέβληαι is epic second-singular perfect middle/passive of βάλλω, corresponding to βέβλησαι: ‘you have been struck.’ κενεών is the flank, accusative of the place supposedly hit. ἀνσχήσεσθαι repeats Pandarus’ earlier prediction that Diomedes cannot hold out. εὖχος is the triumph or boast he prematurely claims.

ταρβήσας is aorist participle of ταρβέω, ‘be afraid,’ negated by οὐ. ἤμβροτες is second-singular aorist of ἁμαρτάνω, ‘missed,’ with the difficult epic stem ἀμβροτ-. ἔτυχες is aorist of τυγχάνω, ‘hit.’ σφῶϊ is second-person accusative dual, ‘you two,’ in the threat continued on the next page.
